summary: Defines a two-way mapping for presence information between SIP and XMPP, so users on the two systems can see each other's availability. It obsoletes RFC 7248.

plainLanguage.summary: Two chat apps speak different languages. This translates the little green dot that says someone is available.

questions: what is sip xmpp presence interworking
how does an xmpp to sip gateway work
how is xmpp presence mapped to sip
what is the difference between a sip subscription and an xmpp subscription
subtitle: How a gateway translates the 'is this person available' signal between SIP and XMPP chat systems.

tldr.problem: SIP and XMPP both carry presence (whether someone is available), but they use different messages, and both use the word 'subscription' for different things. Users on the two systems cannot see each other's availability without a translation.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a bidirectional mapping run by a gateway. XMPP presence stanzas map to SIP SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY requests carrying a PIDF document, and back again, with tables for syntax elements and rules for authorizations, notifications and polling.
tldr.outcome: It covers basic network-availability presence only, not rich presence. It obsoletes RFC 7248, correcting that RFC's architecture of gateways on both sides to one gateway per direction.

today: RFC 8048 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2016. It obsoletes RFC 7248, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction: Presence in Two Worlds
sections.content:
Presence is information about an entity's availability, such as network availability or availability for communication. In both SIP and XMPP it involves a long-lived authorization to receive notifications, an ephemeral presence session while the contact is online, an ephemeral notification session, and the notifications themselves.

Both protocols use the word 'subscription' differently. In SIP it is a short-lived request for notifications that must be renewed. In XMPP it is shorthand for a long-lived presence authorization. To avoid confusion, the RFC says notification dialog for a SIP subscription and presence authorization for an XMPP one.

The RFC maps one protocol directly to the other, because that is how existing systems solve the problem, rather than mapping both to the abstract semantics of RFC 3860, an approach it says apparently was never implemented. Only basic presence is covered; so-called rich presence is out of scope. The intended readers are developers with an existing SIP or XMPP system who want it to talk to the other kind.
sections.plainLanguage: Both apps say 'subscribe' but mean different things, like two languages where the same word means different things. This document picks clear names and then translates carefully.

sections.title: Architectural Assumptions
sections.content:
The basic architecture comes from RFC 7247. This RFC adds that SIP presence can be deployed on the server side in two ways. In the first, a dedicated SIP Presence Server handles the presence event package and tells the user about subscription activity using the presence.winfo package, and the user agent sends updates as PUBLISH messages to the server. In the second, the Presence Server acts as a proxy and just passes SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY through.

Because the XMPP-to-SIP gateway behaves the same in both cases, the diagrams label the far end 'SIP User Agent or Presence Server'. Gateways are abbreviated S2X GW (SIP to XMPP) and X2S GW (XMPP to SIP).
sections.plainLanguage: The SIP side can be run in two ways, but the translator does the same job either way, so the pictures just draw one box for both.

sections.title: Presence Authorizations
sections.content:
XMPP manages authorizations with <presence/> stanzas of type subscribe, subscribed, unsubscribe and unsubscribed, with relationship states none, from, to and both. In SIP the subscriber never explicitly asks for an authorization; it is triggered by a first SUBSCRIBE and the recipient's agent or Presence Server asks the user for a policy decision. The default time-to-live of a SIP notification dialog is 3600 seconds.

XMPP to SIP. An XMPP subscribe becomes a SIP SUBSCRIBE for the presence event. The gateway treats the state as neutral until it gets a NOTIFY with Subscription-State active; for pending NOTIFYs it MUST answer on the SIP side but send no presence to the XMPP user. On the first active NOTIFY it replies 200 OK and sends a subscribed stanza, followed by a presence stanza if the NOTIFY had a body. The gateway renews the dialog and MUST treat SIP responses 403, 489 or 603 as a permanent cancellation, while 423 or 481 are transient. An XMPP unsubscribe becomes a SUBSCRIBE with Expires 0, then the gateway sends unsubscribed and a NOTIFY with state terminated.

SIP to XMPP. A SUBSCRIBE becomes an XMPP subscribe. If the XMPP user approves, the gateway sends an empty NOTIFY with state active. If the user declines with unsubscribed, the NOTIFY has state terminated and reason rejected. Refresh SUBSCRIBEs are answered with a NOTIFY, which MUST be empty if the gateway has no meaningful availability information. SIP has no outbound cancel, so a SUBSCRIBE with Expires 0 ends the dialog, and the gateway sends the SIP agent a closed PIDF status and the XMPP contact an unavailable stanza.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking 'may I see when you are online?' is translated from one app's way of asking to the other's. The answer 'yes' or 'no' is translated back, and saying 'never mind' has its own translation too.

sections.title: Translating Presence Notifications
sections.content:
This RFC focuses on the 'least common denominator' of network availability. An XMPP stanza with no type attribute means available, and type unavailable means not available. A SIP presence notification is a NOTIFY with a PIDF document (RFC 3863). The RFC includes a table for each direction, and the mappings in the tables MUST be followed, while mappings for elements not mentioned are left to the implementation.

Key rules for XMPP to SIP: only stanzas with no type, or type unavailable, become NOTIFYs. These map to PIDF basic status open and closed. The XMPP resource becomes the tuple id, and because a PIDF ID cannot start with a digit it is RECOMMENDED to prefix it with ID- or another alphabetic string. XMPP <priority/> (an integer from -128 to +127) is not mapped when negative, and the RFC gives an example mapping to a PIDF priority between zero and one. XMPP <show/> has no mapping, but the RECOMMENDED approach is to place the element directly inside the PIDF XML in the jabber:client namespace.

In the other direction, PIDF open MUST become a stanza with no type and closed MUST become type unavailable. If the SIP side supports the <show/> extension, the gateway includes it.

An XMPP user may have several clients, each with its own resourcepart, and the SIP agent receives a separate notification from each. How the agent combines them is up to it; typically it shows the 'most available' status.
sections.plainLanguage: The little 'I am here' or 'I am away' badge is turned into the other app's badge, and a few extra details like a status note are carried along when possible.

sections.title: Polling for Presence
sections.content:
Both protocols also let someone ask once for current presence rather than subscribing. In XMPP this is a <presence/> stanza of type probe, sent by servers on behalf of users (clients are discouraged from sending probes). The gateway turns a probe into a SIP SUBSCRIBE with Expires 0 in a new dialog, which makes the contact send a single NOTIFY.

In the other direction, a SIP SUBSCRIBE with Expires 0 is turned by a presence-aware gateway into an XMPP probe if it does not already have presence information about the contact.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking to hear every update, you ask once, 'is she there right now?', and get a single answer.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Detailed considerations are in the SIP and XMPP presence specifications. This RFC adds two points.

First, amplification: each long-lived XMPP authorization typically results in multiple notification dialog refreshes on the SIP side, so an attack from the XMPP network on a SIP Presence Server is possible. Access to an XMPP-to-SIP gateway SHOULD be restricted. Only an XMPP service that carefully controls account provisioning should host one, and a gateway ought to serve only a single domain or trust realm. Before refreshing, the gateway first sends an XMPP probe to the user's bare JID, which puts an equal burden on the XMPP server and the SIP proxy.

Second, presence leaks: presence can be sensitive and can differ between subscribers. A gateway MUST NOT route or deliver a notification to anyone other than the intended recipient, as given by the to address in XMPP or the Request-URI in SIP, because authorization information lives at the user's home service.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator must not be tricked into making too much noise for the other side, and must never pass your 'I am online' news to anyone but the person it was meant for.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 7248
sections.content:
After RFC 7248 was published, the working group found that a related document, since published as RFC 7702, had problems that also applied to it. The diagrams and flows in RFC 7248 showed gateways on both sides of the exchange, which was an incorrect architecture. In practice, XMPP presence is translated by an XMPP-to-SIMPLE gateway and received by a normal SIP system directly, and the reverse for SIP.

This RFC therefore corrects the assumptions, diagrams and flows to a single-gateway model per direction, and changes terminology ('SIP Proxy' or 'SIP Presence Server' instead of 'SIP Server', plus the notification dialog and presence authorization terms). It also clarifies the use of presence.winfo and the Subscription-State values, the durations of dialogs and authorizations, and empty NOTIFYs. It removes the mapping of the XMPP id attribute to the SIP CSeq header, describes multiple connected resources, and adds mitigations for presence leaks.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version drew the translators wrong, with one on each side. This version fixes the drawings so there is one translator for each direction.
